q: What sets Huet's 'Cuvée Constance' apart from the rest of the range?
accept: botrytis selection blended from all three vineyards
sweet vouvray assembled across all three huet vineyards
only huet wine that is not single vineyard
ans: The only still cuvée that is not single-vineyard: a rare selection of botrytis-affected fruit assembled from all three sites (Le Haut-Lieu, Le Mont, Clos du Bourg), first made in 1989 and named for a member of the Huet family
exp: Gaston Huet — the POW-camp wine-lecture legend — defined heroic Vouvray; Constance is the apex sweet bottling, made only in exceptional years.

q: Explain the global decline of sweet wine and one strategy for selling it.
accept: dry preference sugar aversion sell by the glass pair savory
btg pours and savory pairings
ans: Dry-drinking fashion and sugar aversion; sell by the glass, pair with savory (foie, blue cheese, spice), and price the pour honestly

q: Explain how you would judge whether a sweet wine will age.
accept: acidity balance concentration botrytis complexity length
acid carries sugar
~acidity first
~acidity above all
~acidity is the first thing
~start with the acidity
ans: Acidity first — sugar without acid dies; then concentration, botrytis complexity and length. The wine should finish fresh, not cloying
exp: A great sweet wine tastes almost dry on the finish.

q: Explain 'mutage sur grains' and the additional demands made of Banyuls Grand Cru.
accept: fortifying on the skins with grand cru at seventy five percent grenache and thirty months in wood
mutage on the skins extracts colour and tannin banyuls grand cru thirty months oak
grand cru requires minimum 75% grenache noir and long oxidative ageing
spirit added on the skins then rancio ageing
ans: Mutage sur grains means fortifying the fermenting must while it is still on its skins, so the arriving spirit extracts colour, tannin and aromatics at the same moment it kills the yeast — the reverse of mutage sur jus, where the juice is run off first, which is how the white Muscat vins doux naturels are made. It gives red Banyuls and Maury their grip and their capacity to age. Banyuls requires a minimum of fifty per cent Grenache Noir; Banyuls Grand Cru raises that to seventy-five per cent and demands at least thirty months in wood, frequently oxidative — old foudres, or glass bonbonnes left outdoors to bake — which builds rancio, the walnut, coffee and dried-orange character that defines the style. Vineyards are terraced schist above the Mediterranean at Collioure, worked by hand.
exp: The distinction between sur grains and sur jus is the technical heart of the VDN family and explains why red and white examples of the same law taste nothing alike. Rancio is the other half of the answer: deliberate, controlled oxidation as a style, not a fault.

q: What is Eszencia, and what are its legal and physical extremes?
accept: free run juice from aszu berries minimum 450 g/l and barely ferments
minimum 450 grams of sugar with only about two to five percent alcohol
the free run essence served with a spoon
450 g/l minimum sugar aszu eszencia tier abolished in 2013
ans: It is the free-run juice that seeps out of a vat of aszú berries under nothing but their own weight, collected in tiny quantity over weeks. The law requires a minimum of 450 g/L sugar and it frequently exceeds 700. At that osmotic pressure yeast can barely function, so it ferments for years and reaches perhaps 1.5 to 5 per cent alcohol, which is why several markets will not permit it to be labelled simply as wine. It ages effectively forever, is sold in small bottles with a spoon rather than a glass, and was historically the coronation cordial of Hungary, credited with reviving dying kings. Distinguish it from the Aszú Eszencia tier, which was abolished in the 2013 reform.
exp: Eszencia is the outer limit of what fermentation can survive, and the reason it is examined is that it forces you to explain osmotic inhibition of yeast — the same principle that stops every great sweet wine short of dryness. The 2013 abolition of the Aszú Eszencia tier is the current-law detail that catches candidates.

q: Set out the 1855 Sauternes classification and explain the Barsac wrinkle.
accept: yquem alone as premier cru superieur then eleven firsts and fifteen seconds unchanged since 1855
one superior first growth then first and second growths from 1855
barsac estates may label as barsac or sauternes
climens and coutet are classified barsac properties
ans: One Premier Cru Supérieur standing alone — Château d'Yquem — then, after a century and a half of divisions among the original properties, eleven Premiers Crus, including Climens, Coutet, Suduiraut, Guiraud, Rieussec, La Tour Blanche, Lafaurie-Peyraguey, Clos Haut-Peyraguey, Rabaud-Promis, Sigalas-Rabaud and Rayne Vigneau, and fifteen Deuxièmes Crus. It was drawn up alongside the Médoc reds for the 1855 Exposition, on the basis of the prices the wines had been fetching, and like the Médoc list it stands today exactly as drawn. The wrinkle: Barsac is one of the five communes entitled to the Sauternes appellation but also holds its own, so a Barsac estate may label its wine either Barsac or Sauternes as it chooses. Climens and Coutet are classified properties sitting in Barsac, on flatter ground with more limestone beneath, which is the usual explanation for Barsac's comparatively lighter, more incisive style.
exp: Sweet Bordeaux is classified territory and the structure is examinable in itself; the Barsac dual-labelling right is the part candidates fumble. Be ready to add that the classification is a price list from 1855 and predicts quality today only loosely — Yquem's position, however, has stood unchallenged throughout.

q: Commandaria: grapes, method, law and its claim to antiquity.
accept: cyprus xynisteri and mavro sun dried then two years in oak
sun dried grapes minimum two years oak and fifteen percent alcohol
knights hospitaller commanderie at kolossi oldest named wine
xynisteri and mavro dried on the ground in the sun
ans: Cyprus. Two indigenous varieties — Xynisteri, white, and Mavro, red — grown on defined villages on the southern foothills of the Troodos mountains, picked fully ripe and then laid out to dry in the sun on the ground for roughly a week to ten days before pressing. The law requires a minimum of two years' ageing in oak and a minimum of fifteen per cent alcohol; the wine may be fortified or reach that naturally, and traditional producers work a solera-like refreshing system with old mother casks. The name comes from the Grande Commanderie, the Knights Hospitaller's estate at Kolossi, who commercialised it in the medieval period; it descends from the ancient Cypriot 'Nama' described by Hesiod, was reportedly served at Richard the Lionheart's wedding on the island in 1191, and is routinely called the oldest named wine still in production.
exp: Commandaria is the sweet category's deepest cut and a reliable oral probe for whether a candidate's world map extends past western Europe. It also makes a useful teaching point: sun-drying on the ground, rather than mats or racks, is the oldest concentration technique of all, older than botrytis, freezing or fortification.

q: What does Botrytis cinerea actually do to a berry, chemically, and where does the winemaking risk lie?
accept: water loss concentrates sugar it eats acid produces gluconic acid and glycerol and laccase is the oxidation risk
gluconic acid and glycerol with laccase causing oxidation
the mould raises glycerol and secretes laccase which browns the wine
concentration plus glycerol texture and the danger of laccase
ans: The fungus perforates the skin with its filaments, and the berry loses well over half its water to evaporation, concentrating sugar dramatically and acid rather less usefully. The mould metabolises tartaric and malic acid as it feeds, so total acidity does not rise in proportion to sugar; it secretes gluconic acid, which is the analytical marker of botrytis in a lab; it builds glycerol to fifteen or twenty grams a litre, giving the unctuous texture; and it produces both a polysaccharide, beta-glucan, that blinds filters and a factor that inhibits yeast, which is why these ferments crawl and often stop of their own accord — nature doing the job that would otherwise need arresting. It also creates the aromatic register we call noble rot: honey, saffron, dried apricot, and in bottle sotolon. The risk is laccase, the polyphenol oxidase the fungus secretes, which browns and oxidises juice and wine far more aggressively than the grape's own tyrosinase because it shrugs off sulphur dioxide and stays active across a wider pH range. Hence whole-bunch pressing, generous early sulphuring — which restrains laccase without destroying it — cold handling, protection from air, and speed in the cellar.
exp: Advanced candidates know botrytis needs damp mornings and dry afternoons; Master candidates are expected to say what the fungus is doing inside the berry and why the cellar treats the fruit as fragile. Laccase is the operative answer, and the useful detail is what it resists and what it does not: sulphur dioxide only slows it, so botrytised must is pressed whole-bunch, kept cold and away from oxygen and moved fast — heat is the one thing that reliably kills the enzyme, which is why flash treatment is the last resort for a badly affected lot.

q: Define 'zonal vs azonal soils' as vineyard argument.
accept: climate formed in place vs transported
zonal by climate azonal alluvial colluvial transported
ans: Zonal soils weather in place under climate; azonal (alluvium, colluvium, loess) arrive by water, gravity or wind — most great vineyards sit on azonal deposits
exp: Gravel croupes, galets terraces, loess banks: transported all.

q: Contrast the water regime of the clay in Pomerol with Saint-Émilion's côte:
accept: smectite blue clay water regulation limestone slope
crasse de fer smectite swelling clay
ans: Pétrus' smectite ('blue clay') swells shut in rain, rationing water; the côte's limestone-over-clay drains and buffers — two Merlot terroirs, two mechanisms
exp: 'Crasse de fer' iron pan adds the right bank's third variable.
